Then the Boeotians, marching into Phocis with a great force, ravaged most of it and laid waste the possessions in the country; and taking some too of the small towns and gathering a quantity of spoils, they returned to Boeotia.

40.1. In the archonship of Theëllus at Athens, the Romans appointed as consuls Marcus Fabius and Titus Quintius. In their time the Thebans, wearied by the war against the Phocians and short of money, sent envoys to the king of the Persians, asking him to supply money to the city.

40.2. Artaxerxes, readily complying, gave them as a gift three hundred talents of silver. Between the Boeotians and Phocians there were skirmishes and raids of country, but no actions worthy of mention were accomplished in this year.

40.3. In Asia the king of the Persians, having in earlier times marched against Egypt with great numbers of soldiers, had failed, but in the period under consideration again made war upon the Egyptians, and accomplishing notable deeds through his own energy, recovered Egypt and Phoenicia and Cyprus.

40.4. But that we may make the history of these matters clear, we shall set forth beforehand the causes of the war, going back a little to the relevant times. For when the Egyptians had revolted from the Persians in earlier times, Artaxerxes surnamed Ochus, being himself not warlike, remained quiet, but sending forces and generals, often failed through the baseness and inexperience of the commanders.

40.5. Wherefore, being despised by the Egyptians, he was compelled to endure it, both because of his inactivity and the peaceableness of his spirit. But in the period under consideration, when the kings of the Phoenicians and those in Cyprus, imitating the Egyptians, set out, through their contempt, upon revolt, he was provoked and resolved to make war upon those who had revolted.

40.6. Now he rejected the sending of generals, and resolved to make the struggles for his kingdom himself. Wherefore, having made great preparations of arms and missiles and grain and forces, he gathered three hundred thousand foot and thirty thousand horse, three hundred triremes, and five hundred freight ships and other vessels carrying provisions.

41.1. He began to war against the Phoenicians too for the following reasons. In Phoenicia there is a notable city named Tripolis, which has a name fitting its nature; for there are three cities in it, having a furlong's interval from one another; and of these one is called of the Aradians, another of the Sidonians, and another of the Tyrians. This city has the greatest dignity of the cities in Phoenicia, in which it happened that the Phoenicians held a council and deliberated about the greatest matters.

41.2. As the satraps and generals tarried in the territory of the Sidonians, and behaved, in their orders concerning affairs, insolently and arrogantly toward the Sidonians, those ill-used, taking the outrage hard, resolved to revolt from the Persians.

41.3. Persuading also the other Phoenicians to lay hold of independence, they sent envoys to Nectanebo the king of the Egyptians, who was an enemy of the Persians, and persuading him to take them into alliance, prepared the things for the war.

41.4. As Sidon excelled in prosperity, and its private citizens had through their trading acquired great wealth, quickly many triremes were equipped and a multitude of mercenaries gathered, and besides these, arms and missiles and grain and all the other things useful for war were speedily provided.

41.5. Beginning the hostility, they cut down and destroyed the royal park, in which the kings of the Persians were wont to take their rest; then they burned the fodder gathered by the satraps for the horses for the war; and finally, arresting those Persians who had committed the outrages, they took vengeance on them.
41.6. The war against the Phoenicians having taken this beginning, the King, learning of the daring deeds of the rebels, threatened all the Phoenicians, but especially the Sidonians.

42.1. In Babylon, having gathered together the foot and horse forces, straightway he took them up and advanced against the Phoenicians. While he was making his way along the march, Belesys the satrap of Syria and Mazaeus the ruler of Cilicia, joining together, warred against the Phoenicians.

42.2. Tennes the king of Sidon took from the Egyptians four thousand Greek mercenaries, of whom the general was Mentor the Rhodian. With these and the citizen-soldiers, engaging the aforesaid satraps, he was victorious and drove the enemy out of Phoenicia.
42.3. While these things were going on, a war arose in Cyprus too, having its actions intertwined with the war under consideration.

42.4. For in this island there were nine notable cities, and under these were ranged small towns belonging to the nine cities. Each of these had a king who ruled the city, but was subject to the king of the Persians.
42.5. All these, taking thought together and imitating the Phoenicians, revolted, and preparing the things for war, made their own kingdoms independent.

42.6. At which Artaxerxes, provoked, wrote to Idrieus the ruler of Caria, who had just taken over the rule and was a friend and ally of the Persians from his ancestors, to gather a land and naval force to war against the kings in Cyprus.

42.7. He, swiftly preparing forty triremes and eight thousand mercenary soldiers, sent them to Cyprus, putting in command Phocion the Athenian and Evagoras, who in earlier times had been king in the island.

42.8. These, then, having sailed to Cyprus, straightway led the force against the greatest of the cities, Salamis. Throwing up a palisade and fortifying the camp, they besieged the Salaminians both by land and by sea. As the whole island had long been at peace and the country prosperous, the soldiers, mastering the open country, gathered much booty.

42.9. As their abundance was noised abroad, many of the soldiers from the opposite coast of Syria and Cilicia flocked together of their own accord at the hope of gain. At last, the force with Evagoras and Phocion having been doubled, the kings in Cyprus fell into anguish and the greatest fears. And the affairs in Cyprus were in this state.

43.1. After this the king of the Persians, having set out from Babylon with his force, advanced against Phoenicia; and Tennes the ruler of Sidon, learning of the magnitude of the Persian force and thinking that the rebels were no match, resolved to provide his own safety privately.

43.2. Wherefore he sent the most faithful of his servants, Thettalion, secretly from the Sidonians, to Artaxerxes, promising to hand over Sidon and to help conquer Egypt, and to cooperate greatly with him, being experienced in the regions of Egypt and accurately knowing the landings along the Nile.

43.3. The King, hearing the details from Thettalion, was exceedingly pleased, and said he would release Tennes from the charges of the revolt, and promised, if he should do what was agreed, to give him great gifts. But when Thettalion said that Tennes asked also to receive his right hand, at this the King, angered as one not trusted, handed Thettalion over to his attendants and ordered them to cut off his head.

43.4. But when Thettalion, being led away to punishment, said only this, "You, O King, will do what you wish, but Tennes, who is able to accomplish everything, will, because you have not given the pledge, accomplish nothing of what he has promised," again, hearing this, the King changed his mind, and recalling the attendants, ordered them to release him, and gave the right hand to Thettalion; this pledge is the most binding among the Persians. He, then, coming to Sidon, reported to Tennes what had been done, secretly from the Sidonians.

44.1. The King, accounting it of great moment to gain mastery of Egypt because of his former failure, sent envoys to the greatest of the cities in Greece, asking them to campaign together with the Persians against the Egyptians. The Athenians and Lacedaemonians said that they kept their friendship with the Persians, but refused to send an alliance.

44.2. The Thebans, choosing Lacrates as general, sent him out with a thousand hoplites. The Argives sent three thousand soldiers, but did not themselves choose a general, and when the King by name asked for Nicostratus as general, they consented.

44.3. For this man was good both at acting and at counsel, but had madness mingled with his prudence; for being outstanding in bodily strength, he imitated Heracles on his campaigns, and wore a lion's skin and carried a club in his battles.

44.4. Likewise the Greeks who dwelt along the coast of Asia sent six thousand soldiers, so that all the Greek allies came to ten thousand. Before the coming of these, the King, having passed through Syria and arrived in Phoenicia, encamped not far from Sidon.

44.5. The Sidonians, the King having spent time over his preparations, took great care of the supplies of grain and arms and missiles. Likewise they had encompassed the city with three great trenches and constructions of high walls.

44.6. They had also a sufficient number of citizen-soldiers, trained in exercises and toils and outstanding in the good condition and strength of their bodies. In wealth and the other resources the city far surpassed the cities in Phoenicia, and, what was greatest, it had more than a hundred triremes and quinqueremes.

45.1. Tennes, having shared the treachery with Mentor the general of the mercenaries from Egypt, left him to guard a part of the city and to cooperate in the matters of the treachery being undertaken, while he himself advanced out of the city with five hundred soldiers, pretending to be going to a common meeting of the Phoenicians; and he led with him the hundred most notable of the citizens as counsellors.

45.2. When they were near the King, seizing the hundred, he handed them over to Artaxerxes. The King, receiving him as a friend, shot down the hundred as being responsible for the revolt; and when five hundred of the foremost Sidonians came out with suppliant branches, he recalled Tennes and asked whether he could hand over the city to him; for he was very eager not to take Sidon by capitulation, in order that, encompassing the Sidonians with inexorable calamities, he might by their punishment terrify the other cities.

45.3. When Tennes affirmed that he would hand over the city, the King, keeping his anger inexorable, shot down all the five hundred who held the suppliant branches. Then Tennes, approaching the mercenaries from Egypt, persuaded them to bring within the walls both himself and the King.

45.4. Sidon, then, through such treachery, fell into the hands of the Persians. The King, supposing that Tennes was no longer useful, slew him. The Sidonians, before the King's coming, had burned all their ships, in order that no one of those in the city might, by sailing out, provide safety for himself privately; but when they saw the city and the walls seized and surrounded by many thousands of soldiers, they shut themselves up, with their children and wives, in their houses, and set them on fire.

45.5. They say that those then destroyed by the fire, together with the household persons, were more than forty thousand. This calamity having befallen the Sidonians, and the whole city with its inhabitants having been made to vanish by the fire, the King sold the burnt site for many talents;

45.6. for because of the prosperity of the inhabitants, much silver and gold was found melted by the fire. The misfortunes that befell Sidon, then, had such a catastrophe; and the other cities, struck with terror, went over to the Persians.
45.7. A little before these times, Artemisia who ruled Caria died after ruling two years, and her brother Idrieus succeeded to the rule and ruled seven years.
45.8. In Italy the Romans made a truce with the Praenestines and a treaty with the Samnites, but put to death publicly in the market-place two hundred and sixty men of Tarquinii.

45.9. In Sicily Leptines and Callippus, Syracusans having a force, took by siege Rhegium, which was garrisoned by Dionysius the younger tyrant, and expelled the garrison and restored to the Rhegians their independence.

46.1. In the archonship of Apollodorus at Athens, the Romans appointed as consuls Marcus Valerius and Gaius Sulpicius. In their time, in Cyprus, the Salaminians being besieged by Evagoras and Phocion, all the other cities submitted to the Persians, but of Salamis Pnytagoras, being king, alone endured the siege.

46.2. Evagoras was trying to recover the rule of the Salaminians, which was his ancestral, and through the king of the Persians was making his return to the kingdom. But after this, when he was slandered to Artaxerxes, and the King aided Pnytagoras, Evagoras, despairing of the return and having defended himself concerning the charges, was deemed worthy of another, greater command in Asia.

46.3. But having ill administered the rule, he fled again to Cyprus, and being arrested, was deemed worthy of punishment. Pnytagoras, having voluntarily submitted to the Persians, thereafter ruled Salamis without fear.
46.4. The king of the Persians, after the capture of Sidon, the allies having come to him from Argos and Thebes and the Greek cities in Asia, gathered his whole force and advanced against Egypt.

46.5. Coming to the great lake, where are the so-called Barathra, he lost a part of his force through inexperience of the places. But concerning the nature of the lake and the strange occurrence about it, having spoken in the first book, we shall pass over saying the same things twice.

46.6. Having passed through the Barathra with his force, the King came to Pelusium; this is a city upon the first mouth, at the place where the Nile makes its outflows. The Persians, then, encamped forty furlongs from Pelusium, while the Greeks encamped close to the town itself.

46.7. The Egyptians, the Persians having given them much time for preparation, had well fortified all the mouths of the Nile, but especially that at Pelusium, because this was the first and most conveniently situated.

46.8. The place was guarded by five thousand soldiers, with Philophron the Spartan as general. The Thebans, eager to appear the best of the Greeks campaigning together, first and alone dared, hazardously, to cross through a certain narrow and deep canal.

46.9. When they had crossed and were attacking the walls, the guards of Pelusium, pouring out of the city, joined battle with the Thebans; and a great struggle taking place because of the ambition on both sides, they spent the day in the danger and were parted by the night.
47.1. On the next day the King divided the Greek force into three parts, and each part had a Greek general, and beside him a Persian commander, a man preferred for valour and goodwill.

47.2. The first division was held by the Boeotians, having as general Lacrates the Theban, and as Persian commander Rhosaces; he was a descendant of one of the seven Persians who overthrew the Magi, and was satrap of Ionia and Lydia; there followed him much cavalry and not a little infantry of the barbarians.

47.3. The second division was that of the Argives, with Nicostratus as general, and with him a Persian colleague, Aristazanes; he was the King's introducer of suitors and the most faithful of his friends after Bagoas; there were assigned to him five thousand picked soldiers and eighty triremes.

47.4. Of the third division Mentor, who had handed over Sidon, was general, having the mercenaries that were already his; and there campaigned with him Bagoas, in whom the King most trusted, a man outstanding in audacity and lawlessness; he had the King's Greeks and a sufficient multitude of the barbarians and not a few ships.

47.5. The King himself, with the rest of the force, lay in reserve over the whole affair. Such being the division among the Persians, Nectanebo the king of the Egyptians was dismayed neither by the multitude of the enemy nor by the whole arrangement of the Persians, although he was far inferior in number.

47.6. For he had twenty thousand Greek mercenaries, Libyans about as many, and Egyptians, those called among them the "fighting men," sixty thousand, and besides these an incredible number of river boats fitted for the battles and engagements on the Nile.

47.7. He had also fortified the side of the river that inclined toward Arabia, packed with towns, and moreover all divided up by walls and trenches. And having all the other preparations sufficient for the war, he quickly came to grief in the whole matter through his own ill counsel.
48.1. The cause of the defeat was, most of all, his inexperience in generalship and the fact that the Persians had previously been defeated by him in the campaign before this.

48.2. For having then as generals distinguished men, outstanding in valour and military shrewdness, Diophantus the Athenian and Lamius the Spartan, through these he had succeeded in everything; but now, supposing himself to be a sufficient general, he gave no one a share in the command, and through his inexperience could do nothing of what was useful in the war.

48.3. The towns, then, he distributed and guarded with considerable garrisons, while he himself, having thirty thousand of the Egyptians, five thousand of the Greeks, and half of the Libyans, lay in reserve at the most opportune of the entrances. Such being the arrangement on both sides, Nicostratus the general of the Argives, having Egyptian guides, whose children and wives were held as hostages among the Persians, sailed along with the fleet through a certain canal to a hidden place, and landing the soldiers and fortifying a camp, encamped.
48.4. The mercenaries of the Egyptians who guarded the nearby place, as they perceived the enemy's presence, straightway came out to the rescue, being no fewer than seven thousand.

48.5. Cleinias the Coan, having the command of them, drew up the force for battle. The men who had sailed in being ranged against them, a fierce battle took place, in which the Greeks with the Persians, fighting brilliantly, both slew the general Cleinias and cut down more than five thousand of the other soldiers.
48.6. Nectanebo the king of the Egyptians, hearing of the destruction of his own men, was dismayed, thinking that the rest of the Persian force too would easily cross the river.

48.7. Supposing that the enemy with all their force would come against Memphis itself, he resolved to take thought above all for it. He, then, with the army about him, returning to Memphis, prepared the things for the siege.

49.1. Lacrates the Theban, leading the first division, set out for the siege of Pelusium; and turning aside the stream of the canal to other parts, and mounding up the dried-out place, he brought engines against the city. A great part of the walls having fallen, the guards of Pelusium swiftly built others in their stead and raised up considerable wooden towers.

49.2. For some days the wall-fighting being continuous, at first the Greeks in Pelusium stoutly defended themselves against the besiegers; but when they learned of the King's withdrawal to Memphis, being dismayed, they sent envoys about a settlement.
49.3. Lacrates having given them pledges, under oath, that, if they surrendered Pelusium, they should all be conveyed to Greece with whatever they should carry out, they surrendered the fortress.

49.4. After this Artaxerxes sent Bagoas with barbarian soldiers to take over Pelusium; and the soldiers, passing into the place, took away from the departing Greeks much of what they were carrying out.

49.5. As those wronged were indignant and called upon the gods who oversee oaths, Lacrates, provoked, routed the barbarians, and striking down some, came to the aid of those wronged in violation of the truce.

49.6. Bagoas having fled to the King and accused Lacrates, Artaxerxes judged that Bagoas's men had suffered justly, and put to death those of the Persians responsible for the seizure. Pelusium, then, was thus handed over to the Persians.

49.7. Mentor, leading the third division, subdued Bubastus and many other cities and made them subject to the King by a single stratagem. For all the cities being garrisoned by two nations, Greeks and Egyptians, Mentor spread a report among the soldiers that King Artaxerxes had resolved to treat humanely those who voluntarily surrendered the cities, but to those taken by force to deal out the same punishment that he had inflicted on the Sidonians; and he ordered those who guarded the gates to permit any who wished to desert from them.

49.8. Wherefore, the captured Egyptians departing unhindered from the camp, the aforesaid report was quickly spread among all the cities in Egypt. Straightway, then, the mercenaries everywhere fell to quarrelling with the natives, and the cities were filled with strife. For each side, privately, vied with the other to surrender the fortresses and to exchange this favour for hopes of private benefits; which also happened to occur first about Bubastus.
50.1. For when Mentor and Bagoas encamped near it, the Egyptians, secretly from the Greeks, sent someone to Bagoas, promising to surrender the city if they would grant them safety.

50.2. The Greeks, perceiving what had been done, pursued the man who had been sent, and hanging fear over him, heard the truth; provoked at this, they attacked the Egyptians, and slew some, and wounding others, drove the rest into a part of the city.

50.3. The defeated, revealing to Bagoas what had happened, asked him to come quickly and take over the city from them. The Greeks having secretly sent a herald to Mentor, Mentor in secret urged them, when Bagoas should enter the city, to make the attack upon the barbarians.

50.4. After this, when Bagoas with the Persians entered without the consent of the Greeks, and a part of the soldiers had entered, the Greeks suddenly closing the gates attacked those within the walls, and slaying all, took Bagoas himself alive.
50.5. He, seeing his hopes of safety lying in Mentor, begged to be saved, and undertook for the future to do nothing without his judgment.

50.6. Mentor, persuading the Greeks to release Bagoas and to let the surrender be made through himself, took to himself the credit of the success, and having become to Bagoas the author of his safety, made a partnership with him, and giving and receiving oaths about these things, kept the agreement until the end of his life.

50.7. Wherefore it came to pass that these men, being of one mind with the King, were afterward strongest of the friends and kinsmen about Artaxerxes; for Mentor, having been appointed greatest commander in the coastal parts of Asia, rendered great services to the King, gathering mercenaries from Greece and sending them to Artaxerxes, and managing everything in his undertakings with courage and faithfulness;

50.8. and Bagoas, having administered everything for the King in the upper satrapies, so prevailed, through his partnership with Mentor in affairs, that he was master of the kingdom, and Artaxerxes did nothing without his judgment. And after Artaxerxes's death he ever appointed the successors of the kingdom, and had everything of a king except the title. But concerning these matters we shall record the details in their proper times.

51.1. At that time, after the surrender of Bubastus, the remaining cities, struck with terror, were surrendered by capitulation to the Persians. Nectanebo the king, tarrying in Memphis and seeing the cities' impulse toward treachery, did not dare to undergo the dangers for his rule. Despairing, then, of the kingdom, and taking up most of the money, he fled to Ethiopia.

51.2. Artaxerxes, having taken over all Egypt and pulled down the walls of the most notable cities, plundered the temples and gathered a quantity of silver and gold, and carried off too the records from the ancient temples, which later Bagoas ransomed back to the priests of the Egyptians for much money.

51.3. Those of the Greeks who had campaigned with him he honoured each according to his worth with considerable gifts and released to their native lands; and having appointed Pherendates satrap of Egypt, he returned with his force to Babylon, bringing much money and spoils, and having gained great glory from his successes.

52.1. In the archonship of Callimachus at Athens, the Romans appointed as consuls Gaius Marcius and Publius Valerius. In their time Artaxerxes, seeing that Mentor the general had rendered him great services in the war against the Egyptians, advanced him most of his friends.

52.2. Honouring the man with prizes of valour, he gave him a hundred talents of silver, and of his other costly equipment the best; and he appointed him satrap of the coast of Asia and entrusted to him the war against those who had revolted, appointing him general with full powers.

52.3. Mentor, having a connection with Artabazus and Memnon, who had warred against the Persians in earlier times, but were then in flight from Asia and tarrying with Philip, begging the King, persuaded him to release the men from the charges. Straightway he summoned to himself both, with their whole kindred;

52.4. for there had been born to Artabazus, from the sister of Mentor and Memnon, eleven sons and ten daughters. Being delighted at the multitude of children, Mentor advanced the sons, handing over to them the most notable commands in the army.
52.5. He campaigned first against Hermias the tyrant of Atarneus, who was in revolt from the King and held many strongholds and cities.

52.6. Promising to persuade the King and release him from the charges, he came to a parley, and tricking him, arrested him. Gaining control of his ring, and writing to the cities that he had been reconciled to the King through Mentor, and sealing the letters with the ring of Hermias, he sent out with them those who were to take over the places.

52.7. Those in the cities, trusting in what was written and gladly receiving the peace, all surrendered the fortresses and cities. Mentor, then, through deceit quickly and without danger taking over the towns of the rebels, gained great approval from the King, being thought able to conduct generalship practically.
52.8. Likewise the other commanders too who were hostile to the Persians, forcing some and outgeneralling others, he quickly subdued all. And the affairs in Asia were in this state.

52.9. In Europe Philip the king of the Macedonians, marching against the Chalcidian cities, took by siege and razed the fortress of Zereia, and striking certain of the other towns with terror, compelled them to submit; and coming to Pherae in Thessaly, he drove out Peitholaus who ruled the city.
52.10. While these things were going on, in Pontus Spartacus the king of Pontus died after ruling five years, and his brother Paerisades, succeeding to the leadership, reigned thirty-eight years.

53.1. This year having passed, Theophilus was archon at Athens, and in Rome were appointed consuls Gaius Sulpicius and Gaius Quintius, and the hundred and eighth Olympiad was held, in which Polycles of Cyrene won the foot-race.

53.2. In their time Philip, being eager to subdue the cities on the Hellespont, took Mecyberna and Torone without danger through treachery, and marching with a great force against Olynthus, the greatest of the cities in these regions, first defeated the Olynthians in two battles and shut them up in a siege; and making continual assaults, he lost many of his soldiers in the wall-fighting; but at last, corrupting with money the leaders of the Olynthians, Euthycrates and Lasthenes, he took Olynthus, betrayed through these men.

53.3. Plundering it and enslaving the inhabitants, he sold them as booty. By doing this he both provided himself with much money for the war and struck with terror the other cities that opposed him. Honouring with worthy gifts those of his soldiers who had distinguished themselves in the battle, and distributing a quantity of money among those who had power in the cities, he had many traitors to their native lands. And he himself declared that he had increased his own kingdom much more through gold than through arms.

54.1. The Athenians, viewing with suspicion the increase of Philip, came to the aid of those who were ever being warred upon by the king, sending envoys to the cities and urging them to keep their independence and to punish with death those of the citizens who set out upon treachery; and they promised to ally themselves with all, and openly declaring themselves enemies to the king, carried on the war against Philip.

54.2. Most of all did Demosthenes the orator provoke them to take the lead of Greece, being the cleverest of the Greeks in those times. The city, however, was not able to check the citizens from their impulse toward treachery; for such a crop of traitors there was then throughout Greece.

54.3. Wherefore they say too that Philip, wishing to take a certain city outstanding in strength, when one of the natives told him that it was unassailable by force, asked whether even gold could not climb over the wall.

54.4. For he had learned by experience that what was impossible to subdue by arms was easy to overcome by gold. So, setting up traitors in the cities through bribery, and calling those who accepted the gold "guests" and "friends," he corrupted the characters of men by his evil dealings.

55.1. After the capture of Olynthus, holding Olympian victory-festivals to the gods, he performed magnificent sacrifices; and organizing a great festal assembly and holding brilliant contests, he received many of the visiting strangers to his banquets.

55.2. And during the drinking, employing much conversation, and giving cups to many in the toasts, and bestowing gifts upon not a few, and making to all great promises graciously, he had many who desired his friendship.

55.3. And once at the symposium, noticing that Satyrus the actor was gloomy, he asked why he alone thought fit to share in none of his kindness; and when he said that he wished to obtain from him a certain gift, but feared lest, having revealed the request he had in hand, he should fail of it, the king, becoming exceedingly glad, affirmed that he would grant whatever he should ask. And he said that two maidens, of marriageable age, the daughters of a certain guest-friend of his, were among the captives; these, then, he wished to take, not in order to gain any profit from obtaining the gift, but in order that, having provided dowries for both, he might marry them off and not look on while they suffered anything unworthy of their age.

55.4. After this Philip, gladly accepting the request, straightway gave the maidens to Satyrus. And scattering many other benefactions and gifts of every kind, he reaped rewards many times greater than the favour; for many, drawn on by the hopes of his beneficence, hastened, one before another, to give themselves over to Philip and to hand over their native lands.

56.1. In the archonship of Themistocles at Athens, in Rome the consular office was held by Gaius Cornelius and Marcus Popilius. In their time the Boeotians, having ravaged much of the country of Phocis, defeated the enemy near the city called Hya and struck down about seventy of them.

56.2. After this the Boeotians, engaging the Phocians about Coroneia, were defeated and lost many. Then, when the Phocians held some considerable cities in Boeotia, the Boeotians, marching out and destroying the grain from the enemy's country, were defeated on their return.

56.3. While these things were going on, Phalaecus the general of the Phocians, accused of having stolen much of the sacred treasures, was driven from his office; and three generals having been chosen in his stead, Deinocrates and Callias and Sophanes, there was an inquiry into the sacred treasures, and the Phocians demanded an account from those who had handled them; and the one who had administered most was Philon.

56.4. He, being unable to render the account, was condemned, and being put to the torture by the generals, denounced those who shared in the theft, and himself, falling into the utmost tortures, had an end of his life befitting his impiety.

56.5. Those who had embezzled the treasures gave back what was saved and remaining of the theft, and were themselves put to death as temple-robbers. Of the former generals, the first to rule, Philomelus, had kept his hands off the offerings; but the second, called Onomarchus, the brother of Philomelus, expended very much of the god's treasures; and the third, Phayllus the brother of Onomarchus, as general, cut up not a little of the offerings for the mercenaries' pay.

56.6. For the golden bricks dedicated by Croesus the king of the Lydians, being a hundred and twenty, each of two talents, he cut up into coin, and three hundred and sixty golden bowls, each of two minae, and a golden lion and a golden woman, all coming to a weight of thirty talents of gold; so that the whole of the gold cut up, when the treasures were reckoned into silver value, was found to be four thousand talents; and of the silver offerings, both those dedicated by Croesus and all the rest, the generals together had expended more than six thousand talents, and with the golden offerings added, it exceeded ten thousand talents.

56.7. Some of the historians say that what was plundered was not less than that gained by Alexander from the Persian treasuries. The generals about Phalaecus undertook also to dig up the temple, someone having said that in it there was a treasure containing much silver and gold; and they eagerly dug up the area about the hearth and the tripod. The one who reported the treasure produced as witness the most notable and most ancient of the poets, Homer, in the words: "nor all that the stone threshold of the Archer encloses within,
Phoebus Apollo's, in rocky Pytho."

56.8. As the soldiers undertook to dig about the tripod, great earthquakes occurred and struck fear into the Phocians, and the gods openly signifying beforehand the punishment of the temple-robbers, they desisted from the works. The leader of this lawlessness, the aforesaid Philon, quickly paid to the divine power the fitting penalties.

57.1. The Phocians, then, bore the whole charge of the destruction of the sacred treasures, but the Athenians and Lacedaemonians shared in the choice, having allied themselves with the Phocians and having taken pay not in proportion to the number of soldiers sent out.

57.2. So far did this time bring the Athenians to sin against the divine that, a little before the Delphic events, while Iphicrates was tarrying about Corcyra with a naval force, and Dionysius the ruler of the Syracusans had sent to Olympia and Delphi images wrought of gold and ivory, Iphicrates, falling in with the ships conveying them and gaining control of them, sent to the people asking what he should do; and the Athenians ordered him not to examine the things of the gods, but to see how he should feed his soldiers.

57.3. Iphicrates, then, obeying the decree of his native city, sold as booty the adornment of the gods; whereupon the tyrant, angered at the Athenians, wrote to them a letter of this sort: "Dionysius to the Council and People of the Athenians: to wish you well it is not fitting to write, since you commit sacrilege against the gods both by land and by sea, and the images which were sent by us for dedication to the gods you have taken away and cut up, and have been impious toward the greatest of the gods, Apollo at Delphi and Zeus the Olympian."

57.4. The Athenians, then, did such things concerning the divine, and that too while praying that Apollo was their ancestral god and forefather; and the Lacedaemonians, having used the oracle about Delphi, and having through it acquired the constitution admired by all, and even now consulting the god about the greatest matters, dared to share in the lawlessness of those who plundered the temple.

58.1. In Boeotia the Phocians, having three fortified cities, Orchomenus and Coroneia and Corsiae, from these made their campaign against the Boeotians. Being well supplied with mercenaries, they both ravaged the country and, in their attacks and engagements, got the better of the natives.
58.2. Wherefore the Boeotians, pressed by the war and having lost many of their soldiers, and being short of money, sent envoys to Philip asking him to help.
58.3. The king, gladly seeing their humbling and wishing to reduce the Leuctrian arrogance of the Boeotians, sent few soldiers, guarding only against seeming to overlook the plundering of the oracle.

58.4. The Phocians building a fortress about the place called Abae, where there is a holy temple of Apollo, the Boeotians marched against them. Straightway some of them, fleeing to the nearest cities, were scattered, while others, fleeing to the temple of Apollo, about five hundred, perished.

58.5. Now many other divine things befell the Phocians about these times, but most of all that which is about to be told. For those who fled to the temple supposed that they would be saved through the help of the gods, but, on the contrary, by some divine providence they met with the punishment befitting temple-robbers.

58.6. For there being much bedding about the temple, and fire having been left behind in the tents of the fugitives, it happened that, the bedding having caught, so great a flame blazed up, beyond expectation, that the temple and the Phocians who had fled into it were burned alive. For it seemed good to the divine power not to grant to temple-robbers the safety conceded by supplication.

59.1. In the archonship of Archias at Athens, the Romans appointed as consuls Marcus Aemilius and Titus Quinctius. In their time the Phocian War, having lasted ten years, was ended in this manner. The Boeotians and Phocians being humbled by the length of the war, the Phocians sent envoys to Lacedaemon about help, and the Spartans sent out a thousand hoplites, putting Archidamus the king in command.

59.2. The Boeotians having likewise sent envoys to Philip about an alliance, Philip, taking the Thessalians, came into Locris with a great force. Finding Phalaecus again deemed worthy of the command and having the multitude of mercenaries, he prepared to decide the war by a pitched battle; but Phalaecus, tarrying in Nicaea and seeing that he was no match, sent envoys to the king about a settlement.

59.3. An agreement having been made that Phalaecus should depart with his soldiers wherever he wished, he, under a truce, withdrew to the Peloponnese with the mercenaries, who were eight thousand, while the Phocians, crushed in their hopes, surrendered themselves to Philip.

59.4. The king, having unexpectedly ended the Sacred War without a battle, sat in council with the Boeotians and Thessalians. He resolved, then, to gather the council of the Amphictyons and to entrust to it the decision about the whole matter.

60.1. It seemed good, then, to the councillors to give to Philip and his descendants a share in the Amphictyony and to have two votes, which the conquered Phocians had previously held; and to pull down the walls of the three Phocian cities, and that there should be no share for the Phocians in the temple or in the Amphictyonic council; and that it should not be permitted them to acquire either horses or arms, until they should pay back to the god the money that had been plundered; and that those of the Phocians and the others who had shared in the sacrilege who had fled should be accursed and liable to seizure everywhere;

60.2. and that all the cities of the Phocians should be razed and resettled into villages, none of which should have more than fifty houses, nor should the villages stand less than a furlong apart from one another; and that the Phocians should hold the country and bring each year to the god a tribute of sixty talents, until they should pay back the money recorded according to the sacrilege; and that Philip with the Boeotians and Thessalians should hold the contest of the Pythian games, because the Corinthians had shared with the Phocians in the lawlessness against the divine;

60.3. and that the Amphictyons and Philip should hurl down with stones the arms of the Phocians and the mercenaries and burn the remains of them and sell the horses. In accordance with these things the Amphictyons arranged the matters concerning the care of the oracle and all the other things pertaining to piety and the common peace and concord of the Greeks.

60.4. After this Philip, having helped to establish the decrees of the Amphictyons and having behaved graciously toward all, returned to Macedonia, having gained not only a reputation for piety and military excellence, but having also made great preparations beforehand for the increase of power that was to come to him.

60.5. For he desired to be appointed general with full powers of Greece and to carry the war against the Persians; which also came to pass. But concerning these matters we shall record the details in their proper times; now we shall turn to the continuous course of the history.

61.1. We think it just first to record the punishment that came from the gods upon those who transgressed against the oracle; for in general not only upon the perpetrators of the sacrilege, but also upon all who merely touched the lawlessness, an inexorable vengeance followed from the divine power.

61.2. For the architect of the seizure of the temple, Philomelus, in a certain warlike circumstance, cast himself down; and his brother Onomarchus, succeeding to the command of the desperate men, with the Phocians and mercenaries who fought beside him in Thessaly, was cut down and crucified.

61.3. The third, Phayllus, who cut up most of the offerings, being sick of a long disease, could not even be quickly released from his punishment. And last of all Phalaecus, taking up the remnants of the sacrilege, lived for a considerable time in wanderings and great fears and dangers, not in order that he might become more blessed than those who had been impious with him, but in order that, being tortured for a longer time and becoming, through his misfortune, known to many, he might have a calamity that was talked of everywhere.

61.4. For he, after his flight according to the agreement, at first tarried with the mercenaries about the Peloponnese, holding the soldiers together out of the remnants of the temple-plunder, and after this, hiring at Corinth large freight ships and having four light galleys, he prepared for the voyage to Italy and Sicily, thinking that in these regions he would either seize some city or obtain mercenary service; for there happened to be a war between the Lucanians and the Tarentines. And to those sailing with him he said that he was sailing by summons from those in Italy and Sicily.

62.1. When he had sailed out and was on the open sea, certain of the soldiers conveyed in the largest ship, in which Phalaecus himself sailed, fell to talking with one another, suspecting that no one had summoned them; for they neither saw commanders from those who summoned them sailing with them, nor was the voyage a short one, but a long and difficult one lay before them.

62.2. Wherefore, distrusting what was said and fearing the overseas campaign, they banded together, and especially those of the mercenaries who held commands. At last, drawing their swords and striking terror into both Phalaecus and the helmsman, they compelled them to sail back again. The same thing being done also by those conveyed in the other ships, they sailed back to the Peloponnese.

62.3. Gathering at the promontory Malea of Laconia, they found there Cnossian envoys who had sailed from Crete to gather mercenaries; and when these had conferred with Phalaecus and the commanders and given them considerable pay, they all sailed off with them. Putting in at Cnossus in Crete, they straightway, at the first onset, seized the city called Lyctus.

62.4. To the Lyctians, who had been driven from their native city, an unexpected and swift help appeared. For about the same time, the Tarentines being at war with the Lucanians and with the Lacedaemonians, their ancestors, and having sent envoys about help, the Spartans, through their kinship, being eager to ally themselves, quickly gathered a land and naval force, and appointed as general of it Archidamus the king; and as they were about to set out for Italy, the Lyctians asked them first to help them; and the Lacedaemonians, persuaded and sailing to Crete, defeated the mercenaries and saved for the Lyctians their native city.

63.1. After this Archidamus, sailing to Italy and allying himself with the Tarentines, contended in a certain battle brilliantly and was slain, a man praised both for his generalship and his other life, but blamed only for his alliance with the Phocians, as having been most responsible for the seizure of Delphi.

63.2. Archidamus, then, reigned over the Lacedaemonians twenty-three years, and his son Agis, succeeding to the rule, reigned fifteen years. Then the mercenaries of Archidamus, who had shared in the plundering of the oracle, were shot down by the Lucanians, and Phalaecus, driven out of Lyctus, undertook to besiege Cydonia.

63.3. When he had constructed siege engines and was bringing them up to the city, thunderbolts falling, these were burned by the divine fire, and many of the mercenaries, coming to the aid of the engines, were destroyed by the fire; among whom was the general Phalaecus.

63.4. Some say that he, having given offence to one of the mercenaries, was slain by him. The mercenaries who survived, being taken up by Elean exiles, were conveyed to the Peloponnese, and with them warred against the Eleans.

63.5. The Arcadians fighting alongside the Eleans and defeating the exiles in battle, many of the mercenaries were slain, and the survivors, to the number of four thousand, were taken alive. The Arcadians and Eleans dividing the captives, the Arcadians sold as booty all those allotted to them, while the Eleans, because of the lawlessness against the oracle, slaughtered theirs.

64.1. Those who shared in the sacrilege, then, were in this manner deemed worthy of punishment by the divine power. And the most notable cities that shared in the lawlessness, being later subdued by Antipater, lost together both their leadership and their freedom.

64.2. The wives of the Phocian leaders, putting on the golden necklaces from Delphi, met with a punishment befitting their impiety; for one of them, wearing that which had belonged to Helen, fell into the shame of a courtesan and offered her beauty to those who chose to outrage her; while another, putting on that of Eriphyle, when her house was set on fire in madness by the eldest of her sons, was burned alive together with it. Those, then, who dared to despise the divine power were in the manner described deemed worthy of punishment by the gods;

64.3. but Philip, who came to the aid of the oracle, from this time ever increasing more and more, was at last, because of his piety toward the divine, appointed leader of all Greece and acquired for himself the greatest kingdom in Europe. Now that we have sufficiently gone through the Sacred War, we return to the events of another kind.

65.1. For in Sicily the Syracusans, being in strife with one another and compelled to be slaves to many and various tyrannies, sent envoys to Corinth, asking them to send a general who would take charge of the city and put down the greed of those who set out to be tyrants.

65.2. They, judging it just to help their colonists, voted to send as general Timoleon the son of Timaenetus, the foremost of the citizens in courage and military intelligence and, in general, adorned with all the virtues. A peculiar thing happened to befall the man, which helped him toward the choice of the generalship.

65.3. For Timophanes his brother, who excelled the Corinthians in wealth and audacity, had long been openly grasping at tyranny, and at that time, taking up the poor and equipping himself with suits of armour and having the most worthless men with him, went about the market-place, not pretending that he was a tyrant, but performing the deeds of tyranny.

65.4. Timoleon, being most hostile to monarchy, at first tried to persuade his brother to give up his design, but when he would not obey, but ever more strained at the audacity, being unable to set him right by argument, he slew him as he walked about the market-place.

65.5. An uproar arising and the citizens running together, both because of the strangeness and the dreadfulness of the deed, there was strife. For some said that Timoleon, having committed kindred murder, ought to receive the punishment of the laws, while others, on the contrary, declared that the man ought to be praised as a tyrannicide.

65.6. The senate sitting in the council-chamber, and the dispute about the deed being referred to the council, the enemies of Timoleon accused him, while the more well-disposed, speaking on his behalf, advised saving the man.
65.7. The inquiry still being undecided, the envoys from Syracuse sailed in, and revealing their instructions to the senate, asked them to send the general as quickly as possible.

65.8. It seemed good, then, to the council to send Timoleon, and for the accomplishment of the deed they set before him strange and surprising conditions; for they affirmed that, if he should rule the Syracusans well, they would judge him a tyrannicide, but if too greedily, the murderer of his brother.

65.9. And Timoleon, not so much because of the fear hanging over him from the senate as because of his virtue, presided well and beneficially over the affairs in Sicily; for he subdued the Carthaginians, and restored the Greek cities razed by the barbarians to their original condition, and freed all Sicily, and in general, taking over Syracuse and the other Greek cities desolate, made them surpass in populousness. But concerning these matters we shall record the details a little later in their proper times; now we shall transfer our account to the continuous course of the history.

66.1. For in the archonship of Eubulus at Athens, the Romans appointed as consuls Marcus Fabius and Servius Sulpicius. In their time Timoleon the Corinthian, having been chosen by the citizens for the generalship in Syracuse, prepared for the voyage to Sicily.

66.2. He hired seven hundred mercenaries, and manning four triremes and three swift-sailing vessels with soldiers, set sail from Corinth. On the voyage, taking on three ships from the Leucadians and Corcyraeans, he crossed with ten ships the so-called Ionian passage.

66.3. A peculiar and strange thing happened to befall Timoleon on the voyage, the divine power taking part in the undertaking and signifying beforehand the future renown about him and the brilliance of his deeds; for through the whole night a torch went before him, burning in the heaven, until the fleet put in to Italy.

66.4. Timoleon had heard beforehand in Corinth from the priestesses of Demeter and Kore that, in their sleep, the goddesses had foretold to them that they would sail along with Timoleon's company on the voyage to their sacred island.

66.5. Wherefore Timoleon and those sailing with him were exceedingly glad, as if the goddesses were cooperating with them. And dedicating the best of the ships to the goddesses, Timoleon named it "Sacred to Demeter and Kore." The fleet having put in without danger to Metapontium in Italy, a Carthaginian trireme sailed in after it, carrying Carthaginian envoys.

66.6. These, meeting with Timoleon, solemnly charged him not to begin a war nor to set foot in Sicily. But Timoleon, the Rhegians calling upon him and promising to ally themselves, straightway sailed out of Metapontium, eager to outstrip the report about him;
66.7. for he was very wary lest the Carthaginians, being masters of the sea, should prevent him from crossing to Sicily. He, then, hastily accomplished the voyage to Rhegium.

67.1. The Carthaginians, a little before these times, learning of the magnitude of the war that was to be in Sicily, behaved humanely toward the cities allied to them in Sicily, and, putting an end to their quarrel with the tyrants in the island, made friendship with them, and especially with Hicetas the ruler of the Syracusans, because he was the strongest;

67.2. and they themselves, having prepared a great naval and land force, transported it to Sicily, putting Hanno in command. They had a hundred and fifty warships, fifty thousand foot soldiers, three hundred chariots, more than two thousand two-horse teams, and besides these, arms and missiles of every kind and a vast number of siege engines, and an insurpassable quantity of grain and other provisions.

67.3. Coming first to the city of the Entellini, they both ravaged the country and shut up the natives in a siege. The Campanians who inhabited the city, dismayed at the magnitude of the force, sent to the other cities that were hostile to the Carthaginians about help. Of the others, none responded, but those who inhabited the city of Galeria sent them a thousand hoplite soldiers. These the Phoenicians, meeting and surrounding with their numbers, cut down to a man.
67.4. The Campanians who inhabited Aetna at first prepared to send an alliance to Entella because of their kinship, but afterward, hearing of the calamity of the Galerians, resolved to keep quiet.

68.1. Dionysius being master of Syracuse, Hicetas, having about him a considerable force, marched against Syracuse, and at first, throwing up a palisade about the Olympieium, carried on the war against the tyrant who held the city.
68.2. The siege lasting long and the provisions failing, Hicetas withdrew to Leontini (for from this city he set out); and Dionysius, following them and overtaking the rearguard, joined battle.

68.3. Hicetas, turning back upon Dionysius, joined battle, and slaying more than three thousand of the mercenaries, compelled the rest to flee. Using a swift pursuit and bursting in with the fugitives into the city, he gained mastery of Syracuse except the Island. And the affairs of Hicetas and Dionysius were in this state.
68.4. Timoleon, three days after the capture of Syracuse, put in to Rhegium and anchored near the city.

68.5. When the Carthaginians too had sailed up with twenty triremes, and the Rhegians, cooperating with Timoleon, had gathered a common assembly in the city and were making speeches about a settlement, the Carthaginians, supposing that Timoleon would be persuaded to make the voyage back to Corinth, were careless about their guard-duties; but Timoleon, giving no indication of flight, himself remained near the speaker's platform, and secretly ordered the nine ships to sail off as quickly as possible.

68.6. The Carthaginians being distracted in their minds about the Rhegians who were speaking at length as a set-up, Timoleon, unobserved, slipped away to the one ship that had been left and quickly sailed out. The Carthaginians, having been outgeneralled, set out to pursue Timoleon's company.
68.7. But those having gotten a considerable lead, and night coming on, Timoleon's company succeeded in sailing off to Tauromenium.
68.8. The ruler of this city, who throughout had favoured the Syracusans, Andromachus, graciously received the pursued and contributed much to their safety.

68.9. After this Hicetas, taking the best of his soldiers, five thousand, marched against the Adranitae who opposed him, and encamped near the city; while Timoleon, taking on soldiers from the Tauromenitae, set out from Tauromenium, having all together no more than a thousand.

68.10. Setting out at the beginning of the night and accomplishing the march to Adranum on the second day, he unexpectedly attacked Hicetas's men as they were taking their supper; and bursting into the camp and slaying more than three hundred, and taking alive about six hundred, he gained mastery of the camp.

68.11. To this stratagem adding another, he straightway set out for Syracuse, and accomplishing the road at a run, fell unexpectedly upon Syracuse, outstripping those fleeing from the rout. These things, then, were done in this year.

69.1. In the archonship of Lyciscus at Athens, the Romans appointed as consuls Marcus Valerius and Marcus Popilius, and the hundred and ninth Olympiad was held, in which Aristolochus the Athenian won the foot-race. In their time the Romans had their first treaty with the Carthaginians.
69.2. In Caria Idrieus the ruler of the Carians died after ruling seven years, and his sister and wife Ada, succeeding to the rule, governed four years.

69.3. In Sicily Timoleon, having taken the Adranitae and Tyndaritae into alliance, received from them not a few soldiers; and in Syracuse great confusion held the city, Dionysius holding the Island, Hicetas being master of Achradina and the New City, Timoleon having taken over the rest of the city, and the Carthaginians having sailed in with a hundred and fifty triremes to the great harbour and encamped with fifty thousand foot soldiers. Wherefore, while Timoleon's company was dismayed at the multitude of the enemy, an unreasonable and surprising change took place;

69.4. for first Marcus the tyrant of the Catanaeans, having a considerable force, went over to Timoleon, then many of the fortresses, longing for freedom, inclined to him, and finally the Corinthians, manning ten ships and providing money, sent them to Syracuse.
69.5. These things having been done, Timoleon took courage, while the Carthaginians, taking fright, sailed unreasonably out of the harbour and withdrew with their whole force to their own dominion.
69.6. Hicetas being left alone, Timoleon, getting the better of the enemy, gained mastery of Syracuse. Straightway too he recovered Messene, which had gone over to the Carthaginians.

69.7. And the affairs in Sicily were in this state. In Macedonia Philip, having inherited an ancestral enmity toward the Illyrians and having an unalterable quarrel, broke into Illyria with a great force. Ravaging the country and subduing many of the towns, he returned to Macedonia with much booty.

69.8. After this, coming into Thessaly and driving the tyrants out of the cities, he made the Thessalians his own through his benefactions; for he hoped, having these as allies, easily to draw the Greeks too into goodwill; which also came to pass. For straightway the neighbouring Greeks, agreeing with the judgment of the Thessalians, eagerly made alliance with him.

70.1. In the archonship of Pythodotus at Athens, the Romans appointed as consuls Gaius Plautius and Titus Manlius. In their time Timoleon, having struck Dionysius the tyrant with terror, persuaded him to hand over the citadel and, laying aside his rule, to depart to the Peloponnese under a truce, keeping his own money.

70.2. He, then, through unmanliness and lowness of spirit, abandoned in the manner described the celebrated tyranny, which had been bound fast, as they said, with adamant, and lived out his life in poverty at Corinth; and his own life and his change became an example to those who boast foolishly over their good fortunes;
70.3. for he who had four hundred triremes, a little later sailed in a small round vessel to Corinth, conspicuous for the excess of his change.
70.4. Timoleon, taking over the Island and the fortresses that had previously obeyed Dionysius, razed the citadels and tyrant's quarters on the Island, but restored to the fortresses their freedom.
70.5. Straightway too he began to make laws, setting up democratic laws and the rights concerning private contracts, and arranging accurately all the rest, taking very great thought for equality.

70.6. He established also the most honoured annual office, which the Syracusans call the priesthood of Olympian Zeus; and Callimenes the son of Alcadas was chosen first priest of Olympian Zeus, and thereafter the Syracusans continued to date their years by these officials, down to the time of the writing of these histories and the change in their constitution; for the Romans having given the Sicilian Greeks a share in their citizenship, the office of the priests was lowered, having lasted more than three hundred years. And the affairs in Sicily were in this state.

71.1. In Macedonia Philip, wishing to call into goodwill the Greek cities on the coast of Thrace, marched against Thrace. For Cersobleptes the king of the Thracians continued to subdue the cities on the Hellespont bordering on Thrace and to lay waste the country.

71.2. Wishing, then, to check the impulse of the barbarians, he marched against them with a great force. Defeating the Thracians in several battles, he ordered the conquered barbarians to pay tithes to the Macedonians, and himself, founding considerable cities in opportune places, stopped the audacity of the Thracians. Wherefore the cities of the Greeks, freed from their fears, most eagerly enrolled in the alliance of Philip.

71.3. Among the historians, Theopompus of Chios in his Philippic history included three books containing Sicilian affairs; beginning from the tyranny of Dionysius the elder, he went through a period of fifty years and brought it to a close at the expulsion of Dionysius the younger. The books are three, from the forty-first to the forty-third.

72.1. In the archonship of Sosigenes at Athens, the Romans appointed as consuls Marcus Valerius and Marcus Gnaeus Publius. In their time Arymbas the king of the Molossians died after ruling ten years, leaving a son Aeacides the father of Pyrrhus; and Alexander the brother of Olympias succeeded to the rule, with the cooperation of Philip the Macedonian.

72.2. In Sicily Timoleon marched against Leontini; for into this city Hicetas had fled with a considerable force. At first, then, he attacked the so-called New City; but after this, many soldiers being shut up in the city and easily defending themselves from the walls, being unsuccessful, he raised the siege.
72.3. Coming to the city Engyum, which was under the tyranny of Leptines, he made continual assaults, wishing both to drive Leptines out of the city and to restore to the Engyini their freedom.
72.4. While Timoleon was about this, Hicetas, marching out in full force from Leontini, besieged Syracuse, but losing many of his soldiers, quickly returned to Leontini.

72.5. Timoleon, having struck Leptines with terror, sent him under a truce to the Peloponnese, displaying to the Greeks the expulsions of the conquered tyrants. And as the city of the Apolloniatae too was under Leptines, taking over Apollonia, he restored to it and to the city of the Engyini their independence.

73.1. Being short of money for the pay of the mercenaries, he sent out a thousand soldiers with the most distinguished commanders into the dominion of the Carthaginians. These, ravaging much country and bringing back a quantity of spoils, handed them over to Timoleon. He, selling the booty as plunder and gathering a quantity of money, gave the mercenaries their pay for a longer time.

73.2. He gained mastery too of Entella, and putting to death fifteen of those who most favoured the Carthaginians, granted freedom to the rest. As Timoleon increased both in power and in glory of generalship, all the Greek cities in Sicily eagerly submitted to Timoleon, because he restored to all their independence, and many cities of the Sicels and Sicanians and the others ranged under the Carthaginians sent envoys, eager to be received into the alliance.

73.3. The Carthaginians, seeing that their generals in Sicily were conducting the war ignobly, resolved to send out others with great forces. Straightway, then, they enrolled the best of the citizens for the campaign and levied the suitable of the Libyans, and besides these, having got ready a quantity of money, hired as mercenaries Iberians and Celts and Ligurians; and they built warships and gathered many freighters and made their other preparation insurpassable.

74.1. In the archonship of Nicomachus at Athens, the Romans appointed as consuls Gaius Marcius and Titus Manlius Torquatus. In their time Phocion the Athenian subdued Cleitarchus the tyrant of Eretria, who had been set up by Philip.

74.2. In Caria Pixodarus, the younger of the brothers, drove Ada out of the dominion and ruled five years, until the crossing of Alexander into Asia. Philip, ever increasing more, marched against Perinthus, which opposed him and inclined toward the Athenians. Organizing a siege and bringing engines up to the city, he assaulted the walls day after day in relays.

74.3. Constructing towers eighty cubits high, far overtopping the towers about Perinthus, he wore down the besieged from the higher ground; and likewise, shaking the walls with the rams and undermining them by sapping, he threw down a great part of the wall. The Perinthians defending themselves stoutly and quickly building another wall in its stead, marvellous struggles and wall-fightings took place.

74.4. Great ambition being shown on both sides, the king, having many sharp-firing engines of all kinds, through these destroyed those who fought on the battlements, while the Perinthians, losing many each day, received an alliance and missiles and catapults from the Byzantines.

74.5. Being thus again made equal to the enemy, they took courage and audaciously endured the dangers for their native city. The king, however, did not cease from his ambition, but dividing his forces into several parts, fought continuously, in relays, at the walls both by day and by night. Having thirty thousand soldiers and a quantity of missiles and siege engines, and moreover insurpassable other engines, he wore down the besieged.

75.1. The siege lasting long, and many in the city being slain and not a few wounded, and the provisions failing, the capture of the city was expected. Fortune, however, did not overlook the safety of those in danger, but contrived for them an unexpected help. For the increase of the king being noised abroad throughout Asia, the King, viewing with suspicion the power of Philip, wrote to the satraps on the coast to help the Perinthians with all their might.

75.2. Wherefore the satraps, taking thought together, sent to Perinthus a multitude of mercenaries and abundant money and sufficient grain and missiles and all the other things needed for the war. Likewise the Byzantines too sent out the best of their commanders and soldiers. The forces being made evenly matched and the war renewed, the siege again took on an insurpassable ambition.

75.3. For Philip, striking the walls with the rams, continually threw them down, and warding off with the sharp-firing engines those on the battlements, partly burst in through the fallen walls in a mass with his soldiers, and partly mounted by the ladders to the stripped parts of the walls; wherefore, the fighting being hand to hand, some died, and others fell into many wounds. The prizes of victory called forth the valour of the combatants;

75.4. for the Macedonians, hoping to plunder a prosperous city and to be honoured with gifts by Philip, through the hope of profit held firm amid the terrors, while the besieged, having before their eyes the terrors of capture, bravely endured the danger for their safety.

76.1. The nature of the city contributed much to the besieged toward victory in the whole struggle. For Perinthus lies by the sea on a certain high neck of a peninsula, the neck being a furlong across, and it has its houses packed close and outstanding in height.

76.2. These, in their buildings, ever rise above one another along the ascent to the hill and give the shape of the whole city the form of a theatre. Wherefore, though the walls were continually thrown down, they were in no way at a disadvantage; for, walling up the lanes, they used the ever-lowest houses as so many strong walls.

76.3. Wherefore Philip, having with many toils and dangers gained mastery of the wall, found the wall formed automatically by the houses to be stronger. Moreover, all the things useful for war being readily supplied from Byzantium, he divided his forces into two parts, and left half of the soldiers at the siege, putting over them the best commanders, while himself, taking the others, suddenly fell upon Byzantium and organized a strong siege.
76.4. The Byzantines, their soldiers and missiles and other useful things being with the Perinthians, fell into great perplexity. And the affairs of the Perinthians and Byzantines were in this state.

76.5. Among the historians, Ephorus of Cyme here brought his history to a close at the siege of Perinthus; he embraced in his work the deeds both of the Greeks and the barbarians, beginning from the return of the Heracleidae; and he comprised a period of about seven hundred and fifty years and wrote thirty books, setting a preface before each.

76.6. Diyllus the Athenian made the beginning of his second composition the end of Ephorus's history and strung together the subsequent deeds, both those of the Greeks and the barbarians, down to the death of Philip.

77.1. In the archonship of Theophrastus at Athens, the Romans appointed as consuls Marcus Valerius and Aulus Cornelius, and the hundred and tenth Olympiad was held, in which Anticles the Athenian won the foot-race.

77.2. In their time, Philip besieging Byzantium, the Athenians judged that Philip had broken the peace concluded with them; and straightway they sent out a considerable naval force to aid the Byzantines. Likewise the Chians and Coans and Rhodians and certain others of the Greeks sent an alliance to the Byzantines.
77.3. Wherefore Philip, dismayed at the concourse of the Greeks, raised the siege of the cities and made peace with the Athenians and the other Greeks who opposed him.

77.4. In Sicily the Carthaginians, having made great preparations for the war, transported their forces to Sicily. They had in all, together with those already in the island, foot more than seventy thousand, horse and chariots and two-horse teams no fewer than ten thousand, warships two hundred, and freighters carrying the horses and missiles and grain and the rest, more than a thousand.

77.5. Timoleon, learning of the magnitude of the enemy's force, was not dismayed at the barbarians, although reduced to few soldiers. Having a war against Hicetas, he made a settlement with him, and taking on his soldiers, increased his own force not moderately.

78.1. It seemed good to him to set up the struggle against the Phoenicians in the dominion of the Carthaginians, in order that he might keep the country of the allies unharmed, and ravage that under the barbarians.

78.2. Straightway, then, gathering the mercenaries and Syracusans and the other allies, and calling a common assembly, he urged on the multitude with fitting words to the struggle for everything; and all approving his words and shouting to lead them as quickly as possible against the barbarians, he advanced, having all together no more than twelve thousand.

78.3. When he was already in the territory of Acragas, unexpectedly confusion and strife fell upon the army. For a certain one of the mercenaries, named Thrasius, who had plundered the temple at Delphi with the Phocians, and was outstanding in recklessness and audacity, performed a deed in keeping with his former daring.

78.4. For while almost all the others who had shared in the lawlessness against the oracle had met with the fitting punishment from the divine power, as we recorded a little before, he alone, having escaped the notice of the divine, undertook to incite the mercenaries to revolt.

78.5. For he said that Timoleon, being out of his mind, was leading the soldiers to acknowledged destruction; for the Carthaginians being sixfold in number and insurpassable in all their preparations, he promised to defeat them, gambling away the lives of the mercenaries, and not even having paid the pay owed for a long time because of his poverty.
78.6. He advised, then, to turn back to Syracuse and demand the pay, and not to follow on a hopeless campaign.

79.1. The mercenaries gladly receiving his words and trying to make a mutiny, Timoleon, scarcely, after many entreaties and promising gifts, stopped the disturbance. Nevertheless, a thousand having followed Thrasius, he postponed their punishment to another time, and writing to his friends in Syracuse to receive them graciously and pay them, he wholly quenched all the disturbance, but took away from those who disobeyed the glory that came from the victory.

79.2. He himself, restoring the rest by humane intercourse to their former goodwill, advanced against the enemy, who were encamped not far off. Gathering the soldiers into an assembly and through his words instilling courage into the multitude, he went through the unmanliness of the Phoenicians and reminded them of the success of Gelon.

79.3. All shouting, as if with one voice, to attack the barbarians and begin the battle, mules happening to be bringing parsley for the bedding, Timoleon said that he accepted the omen of victory; for the Isthmian crown is made of parsley.

79.4. The soldiers, at Timoleon's order, plaiting crowns of the parsley and putting them about their heads, advanced with joy, as if the gods were signifying victory to them beforehand; which also came to pass.

79.5. For they got the better of the enemy, beyond hope, not only through their own valour, but also through the cooperation of the gods. For Timoleon, drawing up his force, came down from certain hills to the river Crimisus, and ten thousand having already crossed, he dashed against these at the first onset, himself stationed in the middle of the phalanx.

79.6. A fierce battle taking place, and the Greeks being superior both in valour and in skill of hand, there was great slaughter of the barbarians. As those who had crossed were now fleeing, the whole force of the Carthaginians, crossing the stream, set right the defeat of their own men.

80.1. The battle being renewed, and the Phoenicians by their numbers encompassing the Greeks, suddenly a great storm of rain broke from the surrounding sky, and a quantity of large hail, and lightnings and thunders with great winds swooped down; and all these things being driven by the storm against the backs of the Greeks but the faces of the barbarians, Timoleon's men easily endured the occurrence, while the Phoenicians, unable to bear the magnitude of the circumstance, and at the same time the Greeks pressing upon them, took to flight.

80.2. As all turned toward the river, cavalry and foot mingled together, and the chariots confounded along with these, some, trampled by one another and pierced by the swords and spears of their own allies, had a calamity past help; while others, driven in droves by the enemy cavalry into the river's stream and receiving their wounds in the back, died.

80.3. And many were destroyed without an enemy's blow, the bodies being heaped up through fear and the multitude and the difficulties in the stream. But the greatest thing was that, the rains having become violent, the river, borne down with a more forcible current, submerged many and destroyed them as they swam across with their arms.

80.4. At last, of the Carthaginians, those who filled the Sacred Band, being in number two thousand five hundred, and being foremost all of them in valour and reputation, and moreover in property, fighting brilliantly, were cut down.

80.5. Of the others who campaigned with them, there died more than ten thousand, and there were taken captive no fewer than fifteen thousand. Of the chariots, most were shattered in the struggle, and two hundred were taken; and the baggage-carriers and the teams and the multitude of the waggons fell into the hands of the Greeks.

80.6. Of the arms, most were destroyed by the river, but to Timoleon's tent a thousand breastplates and more than ten thousand shields were carried off. Of these, some were later dedicated in the temples in Syracuse, some divided among the allies, and some Timoleon sent to Corinth, ordering that they be dedicated in the temple of Poseidon.

81.1. Much money too having been taken, because the Carthaginians had a quantity of silver and gold drinking-cups and, moreover, surpassing other adornment because of the magnitude of their wealth, he granted to the soldiers to keep all of it as prizes of their valour.

81.2. Of the Carthaginians, those who escaped the danger in the battle scarcely got safe to Lilybaeum. So great a dismay and fear held them that they did not dare to embark on the ships nor sail off to Libya, supposing that, through the gods' enmity toward them, they would be swallowed up by the Libyan sea.

81.3. Those in Carthage, learning of the magnitude of the calamity, were crushed in their spirits and supposed that Timoleon would speedily come against them with his force. Straightway they brought back Gescon the son of Hanno, who had been banished, and appointed him general, because he seemed to excel in audacity and generalship.

81.4. And they themselves resolved not to risk citizen persons, but to gather foreign mercenaries and especially Greeks; and they supposed that many would respond to them for the campaign because of the magnitude of the pay and the wealth of Carthage. To Sicily they sent suitable envoys, ordering them to make peace on whatever terms might be possible.

82.1. This year having passed, Lysimachides was archon at Athens, and in Rome consuls had been appointed, Quintus Servilius and Marcus Rutilius. In their time Timoleon, returning to Syracuse, first drove out of the city all the mercenaries who had abandoned him, those with Thrasius, as being traitors.

82.2. These, crossing into Italy and seizing a certain place by the sea in Bruttium, plundered it. The Bruttii, provoked, straightway marched against them with a great force, and taking the place by siege, shot them all down. The mercenaries, then, who abandoned Timoleon, met with such a calamity as the reward of their own lawlessness.

82.3. Timoleon, having arrested Postumius the Tyrrhenian, who plundered those sailing with twelve pirate vessels and had sailed in to Syracuse as a friend, put him to death. He received also graciously the settlers sent out by the Corinthians, being five thousand in number. After this the Carthaginians, sending envoys and entreating much, he granted them peace, on terms that all the Greek cities should be free, and that the river called Lycus should be the boundary of the dominions of both; and that the Carthaginians should not be permitted to help the tyrants who warred against the Syracusans.

82.4. After this, having subdued Hicetas, he put him to death, and besieging the Campanians in Aetna, destroyed them. And Nicodemus the tyrant of the Centoripini, having struck him with terror, he drove out of the city, and Apolloniades the ruler of the Agyrinaeans, putting an end to his tyranny, made the freed men Syracusans. In general, having rooted out all the tyrants in the island and freed the cities, he received them into the alliance.

82.5. When he had proclaimed throughout Greece that the Syracusans were giving land and houses to those who wished to share in the citizenship in Syracuse, many Greeks came to the allotment; and at last settlers were appointed, to the undivided Syracusan territory forty thousand, and to the territory of Agyrium ten thousand, because of the magnitude and beauty of the country.

82.6. Straightway too he corrected the existing laws in Syracuse, which Diocles had drawn up. And those concerning private contracts or inheritances he left unchanged, but those legislated concerning public matters he corrected, with a view to his own purpose, as seemed at the time to be advantageous.
